explanations.explanation: That's him, friend. The LORD says, "See, I have called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah." Called by name! I've been called plenty of things in my life, mostly "hey, you," and it never once felt like that. Out of every Israelite, God picked this one man and said his name out loud.

Joshua son of Nun was Moses' assistant, and he went up the mountain with Moses (Exodus 24:13). So I see why his name came to mind. But the LORD's pick for this job is someone else. He calls by name "…Bezalel son of Uri…" from the tribe of Judah.

Eliab son of Helon is a name from the tribe of Zebulun (Numbers 1:9), and he isn't in this passage. Easy one to mix up, friend, with all those names flying around. The one God calls by name here is "…Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur…" He's from the tribe of Judah.

I get why you'd think that, friend, because we're talking about a big tent project with lots of serious instructions. But the text never mentions warfare here. God says He has filled Bezalel "…with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship…" This man's job is building, not battles.

Right, friend, and God keeps it all on the building side. He says He has filled Bezalel with the Spirit of God, "…with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship…" Then comes the job list: artistic works in gold, silver and bronze, cutting gemstones for settings, and carving wood (Exodus 31:4–5). Gold, gems and wood, no battle plans anywhere. I'd call that a man you'd trust with a cookie box AND a lampstand.

Yes, and it keeps going! God says Bezalel will "…cut gemstones for settings, and to carve wood, so that he may be a master of every craft." Gold, silver, bronze, gems AND wood. Meanwhile I get nervous when a recipe has two steps.

It's true, friend, and the text says so. After the gold, silver and bronze, God adds that Bezalel will "…cut gemstones for settings, and to carve wood…" Then comes the big finish: "…a master of every craft." Every craft, not just the metal ones.

That's the one. God says, "…I have selected Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, as his assistant." Notice Bezalel is from Judah and Oholiab is from Dan, so two different tribes. God also gave skill to all the craftsmen, so this is a whole team effort.

Nahshon son of Amminadab is listed as a man from the tribe of Judah (Numbers 1:7), and he isn't named here. Long names run together fast, don't they? The one God selects as Bezalel's assistant is "…Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan…"

Elizaphan son of Uzziel was a leader of the Kohathite families (Numbers 3:30), but he isn't the one picked in this passage. Honestly, that name sounds like it needs its own stamp. God says, "…I have selected Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, as his assistant."
That's it, friend. The LORD says, "Surely you must keep My Sabbaths…" After all that talk about building, He turns to rest. Notice He calls them HIS Sabbaths.
This passage isn't about feasts, even though feasts are a good thing to think about. The LORD says, "Surely you must keep My Sabbaths…" Right after the busy building plans, He talks about rest.
Vows don't come up in these verses, friend. What the LORD tells Moses to say is, "Surely you must keep My Sabbaths…" He's talking about a day of rest, not a promise somebody makes.

explanations.answer: He is the LORD who makes them holy
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the point of the sign. God says it's "…so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you." Sanctifies means He makes them holy. The Sabbath is a reminder of who is doing that work, and it's Him.

explanations.answer: He is the LORD who feeds them
explanations.explanation: I love a good provider, but that's not what this sign points to. God says it's "…so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you." Sanctifies means He makes them holy. This verse is about holiness.

explanations.answer: He is the LORD who guides them
explanations.explanation: Guiding is a fine thing for a LORD to do, but it's not named here. God says the sign is "…so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you." That means He makes them holy. Make that one your sign for this verse.

True, friend, and this is a heavy one. God says, "Anyone who profanes it must surely be put to death." He also says, "Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you." The text shows how seriously He treats the day He calls holy.

It's true, friend, and it's a heavy line. The text says, "Anyone who profanes it must surely be put to death." Right before that, God says, "Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you." I won't soften what the text says.
Six it is. God says, "For six days work may be done…" Six days, friend, and then comes the rest. I've stamped a lot of cookies in my time, and I never turn down a day off.
Seventh, yes! God calls it "…a Sabbath of complete rest, holy to the LORD." Complete rest, friend. Even my mustache gets to sit down on that one.
Five is close, friend, but it's one day short. The text says, "For six days work may be done…" Then the seventh day is the Sabbath of complete rest (Exodus 31:15).
The eighth day isn't in this verse, friend. God counts six days of work, and then the seventh is the Sabbath. He says it's "…a Sabbath of complete rest, holy to the LORD." The week stops at seven.

Third is one of the six days when work may be done, so it isn't the day of rest. God says, "For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest…" The day of complete rest comes after those six, friend, on the seventh.

explanations.answer: The LORD made the heavens and the earth in six days and rested on the seventh
explanations.explanation: That's the reason God gives. He says, "for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed." The sign points back to creation. It's a sign between Him and the Israelites "forever."

explanations.answer: The LORD led Israel out of Egypt in six days and rested on the seventh
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't the reason in this verse, friend. God says, "for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed." The reason is creation, plain and simple. Six days of making, then rest.

explanations.answer: The LORD gave all of His laws in six days and rested on the seventh
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. Here God points to creation: "for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed." That's why the Sabbath is a sign between Him and the Israelites.
Stone, friend! The text says they were "…tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God." Written by the finger of God Himself. The story isn't over, either, because there's more to come after this.
Gold is all over this passage, in Bezalel's work, but it's not what the tablets are made of. The text says they were "…tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God." These tablets are stone.

Clay is a good guess, friend, since I know a thing or two about shaping soft stuff. But the text says they were "…tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God." Stone, not clay. The story isn't over, either, because there's more to come.
